Empirical Research Plan: “Is Bank Credit Supply Cyclical—Independent of Loan Demand?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-differences-in-time (DiD) exploiting cross-bank ex-ante vulnerability interacted with aggregate funding stress, while holding borrower-time (“demand”) fixed.

Idea  
•  Each bank has a predetermined, slowly–moving structural exposure to funding shocks – e.g. a high dependence on wholesale funding, low Tier-1 capital, or large pre-crisis securitisation pipeline.  
•  Aggregate funding stress (recessions, LIBOR-OIS, SLOOS net tightening) is plausibly exogenous to any one bank.  
•  When stress rises, “vulnerable” banks should contract credit more than “robust” banks if supply matters.  
•  By absorbing borrower‐quarter fixed effects we compare loans made to the same firm in the same quarter by banks with different ex-ante vulnerability. That wipes out loan-demand and firm-specific macro shocks.

Formally  
LoanOutcome ibqt = β (BankVulnerability b  ×  FundingStress t)  +  γb  +  δfq  +  Xibqt′θ  +  εibqt

β < 0 (for loan volume) or β > 0 (for loan spreads) implies an independent bank-supply cycle.

Why appropriate  
•  Dealscan gives matched borrower–bank panel so we can observe the same borrower borrowing from different banks over time.  
•  Call Reports supply ex-ante vulnerability.  
•  Funding-stress indices are common shocks.  
•  Borrower-quarter FE purges all demand-side heterogeneity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated bank-quarters are those with high ex-ante vulnerability *during* periods of high aggregate stress.

Construction  
BankVulnerability b  = top-quartile wholesale-funding-to-assets ratio measured two years before the quarter t (predetermined).  
FundingStress t       = demeaned, standardised SLOOS net-tightening index (higher = tighter).

Interaction  Treatbt = BankVulnerability b  ×  FundingStress t.

Control group  
Loans from:
1. The same borrower in the same quarter arranged by low-vulnerability banks, and/or  
2. The same vulnerable banks in low-stress quarters.

Treatment timing  
Continuous quarterly panel 1988–2010. Key variation comes from spikes in FundingStress (1990-91, 2001, 2008-09).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Predetermined Vulnerability  
BankVulnerability is fixed long before the stress hits, so it is not chosen in anticipation of the downturn. Compelling: wholesale-funding ratios change slowly and are measured two years earlier.

A2. Common Macro Shock  
FundingStress is aggregate; conditional on borrower-quarter FE it is orthogonal to idiosyncratic borrower events.

A3. Parallel Trends (Conditional)  
Absent the funding shock, lending by high- and low-vulnerability banks to a given borrower would trend similarly. Plausible because we difference within borrower-quarter; we will test pre-trends.

A4. No Simultaneous Borrower Sorting within Quarter  
Borrowers are unlikely to instantaneously drop/choose banks *within the same quarter* in response to vulnerabilities that are largely unobservable to them. Institutional practice (syndicate formation takes months) makes this plausible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous Borrower Sorting across *years*  
Borrowers with better prospects may gradually shift away from fragile banks pre-crisis.  
Mitigation: (i) borrower-*quarter* FE; (ii) test for differential trends 6–8 quarters before stress; (iii) restrict to long-standing bank–borrower matches.

T2. Mis-measurement of Vulnerability  
Wholesale-funding share may proxy for lending appetite, not just funding risk.  
Mitigation: instrument BankVulnerability with long-lagged (e.g. 5-year-ago) mortgage-backed-security holdings, or show robustness to alternative metrics (Tier-1 ratio, unused commitments, pre-crisis ABCP exposure).

T3. Omitted Bank-Level Demand Shocks (Industry Concentration)  
Certain banks specialise in industries hit hard in recessions.  
Mitigation: add Bank × Industry(FIC) fixed effects or interact industry output gaps with time FE.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# PACKAGES
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

#-----------------------------
# 1. LOAD DATA
#-----------------------------
loans   <- fread("dealscan_loans.csv")         # facility-level
banks   <- fread("call_report_quarterly.csv")  # bank financials
stress  <- fread("funding_stress_SLOOS.csv")   # aggregate
compu   <- fread("compustat_firm_quarter.csv") # borrower controls

#-----------------------------
# 2. VARIABLE CONSTRUCTION
#-----------------------------
# Collapse bank balance sheet to quarterly
banks[, wh_funding := fed_funds + repos + brokered_deposits]
banks[, vuln := wh_funding/total_assets]
# 2-year lagged vulnerability (predetermined)
banks[, vuln_lag8 := shift(vuln, 8), by = bank_id]

# Standardise vulnerability within sample
quantile_cut <- quantile(banks$vuln_lag8, .75, na.rm=TRUE)
banks[, high_vuln := (vuln_lag8 > quantile_cut)]

# Merge datasets
setkey(loans, bank_id, quarter)
setkey(banks, bank_id, quarter)
loans <- banks[loans]                       # adds vuln

setkey(compu, gvkey, quarter)
setkey(loans, gvkey, quarter)
loans <- compu[loans]                       # adds borrower controls

setkey(stress, quarter)
loans <- stress[loans]

# Interaction term
loans[, treat := high_vuln * stress_index]   # continuous interaction

# Outcomes
loans[, log_amt   := log(loan_amount)]
loans[, spread_bps:= spread_over_libor*100]

#-----------------------------
# 3. MAIN SPECIFICATION
#-----------------------------
# borrower (firm) × quarter FE => fe = gvkey^quarter
mod1 <- feols(log_amt ~ treat | gvkey^quarter + bank_id, 
              data = loans, cluster = "bank_id")
summary(mod1)

mod2 <- feols(spread_bps ~ treat | gvkey^quarter + bank_id, 
              data = loans, cluster = "bank_id")
summary(mod2)

#-----------------------------
# 4. ROBUSTNESS: ALT STRESS MEASURE
#-----------------------------
loans[, stress_alt := baa_aaa_spread]
loans[, treat_alt  := high_vuln * stress_alt]

robust1 <- feols(log_amt ~ treat_alt | gvkey^quarter + bank_id, 
                 data = loans, cluster = "bank_id")
summary(robust1)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction  
•  β < 0 for loan amount: vulnerable banks cut volumes more when stress tightens.  
•  β > 0 for loan spreads: same banks charge higher prices.

Magnitude (order-of-magnitude prior)  
•  One-SD rise in stress (~10 pp in SLOOS) for a high-vulnerability bank →  
   – 8–12 % decline in loan amounts (elasticity −0.10).  
   – +25–40 bp increase in spreads.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0.5 = partly, 0 = doubtful)

1. Predetermined treatment................................... 0.9  
2. Parallel trends (tested & plausible)...................... 0.8  
3. No spillovers across units................................ 0.7  
4. Accurate measurement of treatment & outcome............... 0.8  
5. Robustness to alternative specifications.................. 0.9  
                                                             -----
Overall (mean)............................................... 0.82
